provenance: Opus 5.5 subscription CLI draft with host review/repairs, source restrictions and execution verification.

draft_notes.explanation:
Original mechanism: build a block from a left-right mirrored copy followed by the original, i.e. [fliplr(g) | g], doubling the width. Then stack [flipud(block); block; flipud(block)], tripling the height.

I tracked how the original column direction (0,+1) moves under the D4 transform. A reflection maps (dr,dc) to (dr,-dc), and a clockwise rotation maps (dr,dc) to (dc,-dr). This decides two things:
- Which visible axis carries the doubling: columns for d4 in {0,2,4,6}, rows for d4 in {1,3,5,7}.
- Whether the unmirrored copy sits at the high end (d4 in {0,1,6,7}) or the low end (d4 in {2,3,4,5}).

The tripling (flip, block, flip) runs along the other visible axis. It is unchanged if that axis is reversed, because reversing [F,B,F] with a flipped input gives the same pattern.

The emitted program works directly in visible coordinates using numpy slicing. It concatenates along the chosen axis and does no rotation or normalization. No colour roles exist: every cell is copied as-is, so the palette needs no handling.
draft_notes.limitations: The program ignores the demonstrations. It assumes every episode follows the constructor's fixed mirror and tile layout, which the D4 index fully determines. It accepts any rectangular input size (the constructor uses 3x2), and the output is 3H x 2W in the original orientation's axes. The fixtures and constructor agree with this uniform rule. I found no constructor defects or hidden tie-breaks. I have not run any tests.
